steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Earth is an oblate spheroid: slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator due to rotation. Its polar diameter is about 12,714 km and equatorial diameter about 12,756 km.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Evidence for a spherical Earth: ships disappear hull-first over the horizon; circular shadow on the Moon during a lunar eclipse; different constellations visible at different latitudes; photographs from space.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Eratosthenes (c.240 BC) estimated Earth's circumference by measuring the angle of the Sun at different latitudes and using the distance between them, obtaining a value close to 40,000 km.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Earth's internal structure: inner core (solid iron-nickel, ~5,150 km depth), outer core (liquid iron-nickel, ~2,890 km), mantle (semi-solid silicate rock, ~35 km), crust (solid rock, 5-70 km).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know Eratosthenes' method in detail — it is frequently examined and requires explaining the geometry of the measurement. Always specify that the Earth is an oblate spheroid, not a perfect sphere. For seismic wave questions, be precise: P-waves refract at the core boundary; S-waves are absorbed by the liquid outer core. When discussing atmospheric effects, distinguish between refraction (bending light), scattering (dispersing light), and absorption (blocking light).
